Limitation
What it means in practice
Technical
The app's own state is in memory
Restarting clears every account, booking and code. A demonstration has to be done in one sitting
Technical
The community membership list lives in the app, not on the server
Accounts persist and the list that decides who may hold one does not. FR1's eligibility check was never moved to a function, so the two halves of registration are stored in different places
Technical
Accounts and bookings are mirrored to the server, not moved there

The same record is written twice and the two writes are not atomic. If the second write fails there is no retry and no reconciliation, so the app shows a booking the server cannot see, and that booking silently cannot produce a code. Nothing detects the divergence. Highest-priority technical debt
Technical
Cloud functions run in the emulator, not deployed
Cold starts, region latency, secret rotation and deploy-time failures are all untested. These are exactly the failures that only appear in production
Technical
No physical cabinet, Android only, on an emulator
The messaging contract, signing, expiry and duplicate handling are real; the actuator is not. No valid timing, frame-rate or battery figures. iOS needs macOS and a paid developer account
Process
One developer, no reviewer
Every design decision was reviewed by the person who made it. The hand-over defect survived because the only person exercising the feature was the person who specified it
Process
Three one-week sprints compressed into 23 days
No gap between building a feature and returning to it. Three of the four wording defects were found by reading screenshots, not by use
Process
The environment cost more than planned, twice

Seven faults blocked the end-to-end run: a stale emulator process, a JDK not on the path, a mistyped secret filename, orphaned ports. The same shape as the five in Sprint 0, after a paragraph had already been written about them
Evaluation
The interface blocks the paths the server is designed to refuse
Three of twelve end-to-end steps could not be run through the app at all. Server refusals are covered by unit tests in both languages, not end to end
Evaluation
The stand-in backend cannot refuse a credential as not the presenter's

With no signed-in caller it infers the presenter from the credential it is shown, so the ownership rule holds there by construction. This is why the hand-over defect survived 430 tests, and the same blind spot covers every identity rule
Evaluation
One evaluator, who is also the developer, and no resident

A single inspector finds roughly a third of what five would, and an author scores their own work generously. Nobody outside the project has used the system, so every usability result here is an inspection finding and none is user validation. The two people in Appendix A are design personas, not participants
Evaluation
Coverage measures execution, not correctness
91% of lines ran at least once. The hand-over defect was in lines that ran
